claim: Next-generation immune-based therapies are expected to facilitate the eradication of intractable pathogens, cancer and autoimmune diseases.
source: Next-generation immune-based therapies are expected to facilitate the eradication of intractable pathogens, cancer and autoimmune diseases (Koff et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Koff et al., 2013

claim: T cells play a critical role in immune-based therapies by their ability to detect the presence of disease-specific antigens/peptides presented by MHC molecules.
source: T cells play a critical role in such therapies by their ability to detect the presence of disease-specific antigens/peptides presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules (human leukocyte antigen [HLA] molecules in humans).
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about T cell function

claim: HLA class I-associated peptides are 8–12 amino acids in length.
source: Under steady-state or pathological conditions, thousands of HLA class I-associated peptides of 8–12 amino acids in length are displayed on the surface of virtually all nucleated cells for scrutiny by CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HLA class I peptide length

claim: HLA class I-associated peptides are displayed on the surface of virtually all nucleated cells for scrutiny by CD8+ T cells.
source: Under steady-state or pathological conditions, thousands of HLA class I-associated peptides of 8–12 amino acids in length are displayed on the surface of virtually all nucleated cells for scrutiny by CD8+ T cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HLA class I presentation

claim: HLA class II-associated peptides are 10–25 amino acids in length.
source: HLA class II-associated peptides are 10–25 amino acids in length and are normally found on the surface of specialized antigen-presenting cells including macrophages and dendritic cells for presentation to CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HLA class II peptide length

claim: HLA class II-associated peptides are normally found on the surface of specialized antigen-presenting cells including macrophages and dendritic cells for presentation to CD4+ T cells.
source: HLA class II-associated peptides are 10–25 amino acids in length and are normally found on the surface of specialized antigen-presenting cells including macrophages and dendritic cells for presentation to CD4+ T cells.
evidence: Established scientific knowledge about HLA class II presentation

claim: There are more than 3000 HLA alleles in the human population.
source: The composition of the immunopeptidome in the human population is complicated by the presence of more than 3000 HLA alleles, resulting in a high diversity of peptide repertoires characterized by the presence of HLA allele-specific binding motifs (Falk et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falk et al., 1991

claim: HLA alleles result in a high diversity of peptide repertoires characterized by the presence of HLA allele-specific binding motifs.
source: The composition of the immunopeptidome in the human population is complicated by the presence of more than 3000 HLA alleles, resulting in a high diversity of peptide repertoires characterized by the presence of HLA allele-specific binding motifs (Falk et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Falk et al., 1991

claim: Mass spectrometry has evolved as the method of choice for the exploration of the human immunopeptidome.
source: Mass spectrometry (MS) has evolved as the method of choice for the exploration of the human immunopeptidome (Hunt et al., 1992; Admon and Bassani-Sternberg, 2011; Granados et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The largest HLA peptidomes reported to date using MS contain more than 10,000 class I or class II peptides.
source: The largest HLA peptidomes reported to date using MS contain more than 10,000 class I or class II peptides (Hassan et al., 2013; Bergseng et al., 2014; Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hassan et al., 2013; Bergseng et al., 2014; Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015

claim: Individual peptides are expressed on average at 50 copies per cell with extremes ranging from 1 to 10,000 copies per cell.
source: Estimates from various analytical and cell-based techniques also indicate that individual peptides are expressed on average at 50 copies per cell with extremes ranging from 1 to 10,000 copies per cell (Granados et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Granados et al., 2015

claim: As many as 84% of peptides may remain unselected for fragmentation in DDA analyses of complex/unfractionated digests of cell lysate even though they are clearly detectable by the mass spectrometer.
source: In fact, analyses of complex/unfractionated digests of cell lysate using DDA have shown that as many as 84% of peptides may remain unselected for fragmentation even though they are clearly detectable by the mass spectrometer (Michalski et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Michalski et al., 2011

claim: As many as 20% of the selected HLA peptides can vary between replicate analyses of the same sample.
source: Although the complexity of isolated HLA peptides is hardly comparable with that of cell lysate digests, as many as 20% of the selected HLA peptides can vary between replicate analyses of the same sample (Granados et al., 2014) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Granados et al., 2014 and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: S/MRM is limited by its capacity to detect only tens to hundreds of peptides per sample injection.
source: S/MRM is, however, limited by its capacity to detect only tens to hundreds of peptides per sample injection and thus is not ideally suited to comprehensively quantify HLA peptidomes.
evidence: Established limitation of S/MRM technique

claim: SWATH-MS combines data-independent acquisition (DIA) with a targeted data extraction strategy.
source: To overcome this limitation, we recently introduced SWATH-MS, a new mass spectrometric technique that combines data-independent acquisition (DIA) with a targeted data extraction strategy (Gillet et al., 2012; Röst et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Gillet et al., 2012; Röst et al., 2014

claim: In DIA mode, all peptides in a sample are fragmented and the corresponding fragment ion spectra are acquired.
source: In DIA mode, all peptides in a sample are fragmented and the corresponding fragment ion spectra are acquired, resulting in a digital recording of the peptide sample.
evidence: Description of DIA methodology

claim: DIA is an unbiased MS technique that represents a suitable strategy for efficiently generating consistent, reproducible and quantitatively accurate measurements of peptides across multiple samples.
source: DIA is an unbiased MS technique and therefore represents a suitable strategy for efficiently generating consistent, reproducible and quantitatively accurate measurements of peptides across multiple samples (Gillet et al., 2012; Collins et al., 2013; Rosenberger et al., 2014; Röst et al., 2014; Guo et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2015; Schubert et al., 2015a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: High-quality assay libraries are required to extract quantitative information from digital SWATH-MS data.
source: To extract quantitative information from digital SWATH-MS data, high-quality assay libraries are required.
evidence: Established requirement for SWATH-MS analysis

claim: Assay libraries contain retention-time and fragmentation information of the peptides to be targeted.
source: Such libraries contain retention-time and fragmentation information of the peptides to be targeted.
evidence: Description of assay library contents

claim: Assay libraries are generated from native and/or synthetic peptides using a SWATH compatible mass spectrometer operated in DDA mode.
source: Assay libraries are generated from native and/or synthetic peptides using a SWATH compatible mass spectrometer operated in DDA mode.
evidence: Description of assay library generation methodology

claim: Generic SWATH assay libraries were generated for Mycobacterium tuberculosis.
source: These include Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Schubert et al., 2015a), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Selevsek et al., 2015), and Homo sapiens (Rosenberger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schubert et al., 2015a

claim: Generic SWATH assay libraries were generated for Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
source: These include Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Schubert et al., 2015a), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Selevsek et al., 2015), and Homo sapiens (Rosenberger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Selevsek et al., 2015

claim: Generic SWATH assay libraries were generated for Homo sapiens.
source: These include Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Schubert et al., 2015a), Saccharomyces cerevisiae (Selevsek et al., 2015), and Homo sapiens (Rosenberger et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rosenberger et al., 2014

claim: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in viral infection contexts.
source: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in various contexts—that is, viral infection (Croft et al., 2013), autoimmunity (Schittenhelm et al., 2014a) and cancer (Gubin et al., 2014)—but have never been created for robust quantitative and high-throughput measurement of HLA-associated peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Supported by citation to Croft et al., 2013

claim: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in autoimmunity contexts.
source: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in various contexts—that is, viral infection (Croft et al., 2013), autoimmunity (Schittenhelm et al., 2014a) and cancer (Gubin et al., 2014)—but have never been created for robust quantitative and high-throughput measurement of HLA-associated peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schittenhelm et al., 2014a

claim: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in cancer contexts.
source: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in various contexts—that is, viral infection (Croft et al., 2013), autoimmunity (Schittenhelm et al., 2014a) and cancer (Gubin et al., 2014)—but have never been created for robust quantitative and high-throughput measurement of HLA-associated peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Supported by citation to Gubin et al., 2014

claim: Assay libraries have never been created for robust quantitative and high-throughput measurement of HLA-associated peptides by SWATH-MS prior to this study.
source: Assay libraries were successfully employed to measure a limited number of MHC class I peptides by S/MRM in various contexts—that is, viral infection (Croft et al., 2013), autoimmunity (Schittenhelm et al., 2014a) and cancer (Gubin et al., 2014)—but have never been created for robust quantitative and high-throughput measurement of HLA-associated peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Statement of novelty of the current work

claim: The study developed a workflow to generate a pilot repository of HLA allele-specific peptide spectral and assay libraries.
source: Towards this end, we developed a workflow to (1) generate a pilot repository of HLA allele-specific peptide spectral and assay libraries, and to (2) analyze SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data acquired from multiple international laboratories (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of study objectives with reference to Figure 1

claim: The study developed a workflow to analyze SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data acquired from multiple international laboratories.
source: Towards this end, we developed a workflow to (1) generate a pilot repository of HLA allele-specific peptide spectral and assay libraries, and to (2) analyze SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data acquired from multiple international laboratories (Figure 1).
evidence: Description of study objectives with reference to Figure 1

claim: Libraries were created from natural and/or synthetic HLA class I and II peptides.
source: In this study, libraries were created from natural and/or synthetic HLA class I and II peptides whereas analysis of SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data focused mainly on naturally presented class I peptides.
evidence: Description of study methodology

claim: Analysis of SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data focused mainly on naturally presented class I peptides.
source: In this study, libraries were created from natural and/or synthetic HLA class I and II peptides whereas analysis of SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data focused mainly on naturally presented class I peptides.
evidence: Description of study scope

claim: HLA class I peptides were isolated from JYEBV+ cells and analyzed in six technical replicates by DDA, with 40% of peptides found in all analyses.
source: HLA class I peptides were isolated from JYEBV+ cells. Six technical replicates were consecutively injected in a TripleTOF 5600 MS. The Venn diagrams indicate the number of peptides identified in each analysis and the number of peptides shared between the runs. (A) Three datasets were acquired in DDA mode and the peptides were identified using the open source database search engines (1% peptide-level FDR).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A

claim: HLA class I peptides were isolated from JYEBV+ cells and analyzed in six technical replicates by SWATH-MS, with 97% of peptides found in all analyses.
source: (B) Three datasets were acquired in SWATH mode and the peptides were identified using OpenSWATH and a combined HLA-A and -B peptide assay library (1% peptide-level FDR).
evidence: Data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B

claim: The study created a computational workflow to support the identification, classification/annotation, visualization and storage of HLA peptidomic data in an allele-dependent manner.
source: Here, we first created a computational workflow to support the identification, classification/annotation, visualization and storage of HLA peptidomic data in an allele-dependent manner.
evidence: Description of computational workflow development

claim: The software tools enable systematic annotation of peptides to their respective HLA allele.
source: The software tools described in the section below enable (1) systematic annotation of peptides to their respective HLA allele, (2) visualization of HLA peptidomic datasets, and (3) generation of HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries, which can be converted into high quality assay libraries for the processing of SWATH-data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of software capabilities with reference to figures

claim: The software tools enable visualization of HLA peptidomic datasets.
source: The software tools described in the section below enable (1) systematic annotation of peptides to their respective HLA allele, (2) visualization of HLA peptidomic datasets, and (3) generation of HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries, which can be converted into high quality assay libraries for the processing of SWATH-data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of software capabilities with reference to figures

claim: The software tools enable generation of HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries.
source: The software tools described in the section below enable (1) systematic annotation of peptides to their respective HLA allele, (2) visualization of HLA peptidomic datasets, and (3) generation of HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries, which can be converted into high quality assay libraries for the processing of SWATH-data (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 2 and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of software capabilities with reference to figures

claim: HLA class I-bound peptides were isolated from fourteen PBMC samples expressing different combinations of HLA class I alleles.
source: To test our workflow, the generated data and computational resources, we first assessed the feasibility of generating HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries from a panel of fourteen PBMC samples (PBMC #1–14) expressing different combinations of HLA class I alleles.
evidence: Description of experimental design

claim: HLA class I-bound peptides from PBMC samples were analyzed by DDA on an Orbitrap-XL mass spectrometer.
source: HLA class I-bound peptides were isolated from HLA-typed PBMC's by immunoaffinity chromatography and analyzed by DDA on an Orbitrap-XL mass spectrometer (Figure 2 and Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Description of experimental methodology with reference to figures

claim: Peptides were identified using multiple open-source database search engines and the search identifications were combined and statistically scored using PeptideProphet and iProphet within the Trans-Proteomic Pipeline.
source: Peptides were identified using multiple open-source database search engines. The search identifications were combined and statistically scored using PeptideProphet and iProphet within the Trans-Proteomic Pipeline (TPP) as shown previously (Figure 1) (Shteynberg et al., 2011, 2013).
evidence: Description of data analysis methodology with citations

claim: The study designed a fully automated annotation strategy integrating the stand-alone software package of the HLA binding prediction algorithm NetMHC 3.4 with a set of in-house software tools.
source: Here, we designed a fully automated annotation strategy integrating the stand-alone software package of the HLA binding prediction algorithm NetMHC 3.4 with a set of in-house software tools (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Description of computational method development with reference to figure

claim: The in-house software tools enable an automated, consistent and effective annotation of the majority of the identified peptides to their respective HLA allele.
source: The in-house software tools enable an automated, consistent and effective annotation of the majority of the identified peptides to their respective HLA allele (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Description of software performance

claim: Each identified peptide was given a predicted HLA binding affinity (IC50) for each of the HLA alleles expressed in the corresponding healthy donor.
source: Briefly, each identified peptide was given a predicted HLA binding affinity (IC50) for each of the HLA alleles expressed in the corresponding healthy donor.
evidence: Description of annotation methodology

claim: An HLA annotation score was computed for each individual peptide by dividing its second best IC50 value by its best IC50 value.
source: An HLA annotation score was then computed for each individual peptide by dividing its second best IC50 value (i.e., the second best predicted allele) by its best IC50 value (i.e., the best predicted allele).
evidence: Description of annotation scoring methodology

claim: Peptides with an HLA annotation score ≥3 were systematically annotated to the allele predicted to bind best.
source: Peptides with an HLA annotation score ≥3 (selected cutoff value; see 'Materials and methods' and Supplementary file 1) were systematically annotated to the allele predicted to bind best (e.g., HLA-A03 for the KLEEQARAK peptide).
evidence: Description of annotation criteria

claim: Using the scoring strategy, ∼80% of all identified 8–12-mers were annotated to a specific HLA-A or -B allele.
source: Using this scoring strategy, ∼80% of all identified 8–12-mers were annotated to a specific HLA-A or -B allele (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to source data

claim: HLA-A and -B alleles were prioritized due to the high reliability of the NetMHC 3.4 predictor for a broad diversity of HLA-A and -B alleles as well as for their high expression levels.
source: HLA-A and -B alleles were prioritized due to the high reliability of the NetMHC 3.4 predictor for a broad diversity of HLA-A and -B alleles as well as for their high expression levels (Kim et al., 2014; Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015; Trolle et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim et al., 2014; Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015; Trolle et al., 2015

claim: A corrected false discovery rate (cFDR) was estimated for each PBMC sample following removal of all non-annotated contaminant peptides.
source: A corrected false discovery rate (cFDR) was estimated for each PBMC sample following removal of all non-annotated contaminant peptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), resulting in a total of 4153 (peptide-level FDR 1%; average cFDR 0.5%) or 7921 (peptide-level FDR 5%; average cFDR 2.5%) distinct annotated peptides distributed across eighteen HLA class I alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: At peptide-level FDR 1%, a total of 4153 distinct annotated peptides were identified with an average cFDR of 0.5%.
source: A corrected false discovery rate (cFDR) was estimated for each PBMC sample following removal of all non-annotated contaminant peptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), resulting in a total of 4153 (peptide-level FDR 1%; average cFDR 0.5%) or 7921 (peptide-level FDR 5%; average cFDR 2.5%) distinct annotated peptides distributed across eighteen HLA class I alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: At peptide-level FDR 5%, a total of 7921 distinct annotated peptides were identified with an average cFDR of 2.5%.
source: A corrected false discovery rate (cFDR) was estimated for each PBMC sample following removal of all non-annotated contaminant peptides (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3), resulting in a total of 4153 (peptide-level FDR 1%; average cFDR 0.5%) or 7921 (peptide-level FDR 5%; average cFDR 2.5%) distinct annotated peptides distributed across eighteen HLA class I alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: All annotated peptides identified from the 14 PBMC samples were used in SpectraST to build the HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries.
source: All annotated peptides identified from the 14 PBMC samples were then used in SpectraST (Lam et al., 2008) to build the HLA class I allele-specific peptide spectral libraries ('Materials and methods').
evidence: Description of library generation methodology with citation

claim: Endogenous HLA-C04 peptides were shown to be significantly expressed on the surface of C1R cells.
source: Notably, endogenous HLA-C04 peptides were recently shown to be significantly expressed on the surface of C1R cells (Schittenhelm et al., 2014b) and were therefore considered in this study.
evidence: Supported by citation to Schittenhelm et al., 2014b

claim: A total of 3528 HLA-A peptides, 4208 HLA-B peptides and 205 HLA-C04 peptides were recorded in the spectral libraries.
source: In total, 3528 HLA-A peptides, 4208 HLA-B peptides and 205 HLA-C04 peptides were recorded in the spectral libraries, which were then stored in the public PeptideAtlas database (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Data summary with reference to source data

claim: The spectral libraries were stored in the public PeptideAtlas database.
source: In total, 3528 HLA-A peptides, 4208 HLA-B peptides and 205 HLA-C04 peptides were recorded in the spectral libraries, which were then stored in the public PeptideAtlas database (Figure 2—source data 4).
evidence: Description of data storage with reference to source data

claim: Naturally presented and/or synthetic HLA class I and class II peptides were provided from six independent laboratories.
source: Here, we aimed at initiating a worldwide community-based effort to generate pilot HLA allele-specific peptide assay libraries that could be further used for the analysis of SWATH-MS HLA peptidomic data. Naturally presented and/or synthetic HLA class I and class II peptides were provided from six independent laboratories and were analyzed using four distinct TripleTOF 5600 MS instruments operated in DDA acquisition mode in four different international institutions.
evidence: Description of collaborative study design

claim: Peptides were analyzed using four distinct TripleTOF 5600 MS instruments operated in DDA acquisition mode in four different international institutions.
source: Naturally presented and/or synthetic HLA class I and class II peptides were provided from six independent laboratories and were analyzed using four distinct TripleTOF 5600 MS instruments operated in DDA acquisition mode in four different international institutions.
evidence: Description of multi-site experimental design

claim: All laboratories used the spiked-in landmark iRT peptides for retention time normalization.
source: All laboratories used the spiked-in landmark iRT peptides for retention time normalization (Escher et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of standardization methodology with citation

claim: The DDA data generated by different groups resulted in the identification of 7668 distinct HLA class I peptides at peptide-level FDR 1% with an average cFDR of 0.5%.
source: The DDA data generated by the different groups were shared and pipelined through the computational workflow described above, resulting in the identification of 7668 (peptide-level FDR 1%; average cFDR 0.5%) or 11,275 (peptide-level FDR 5%; average cFDR 2.5%) distinct HLA class I peptides distributed across eleven different HLA class I alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: The DDA data generated by different groups resulted in the identification of 11,275 distinct HLA class I peptides at peptide-level FDR 5% with an average cFDR of 2.5%.
source: The DDA data generated by the different groups were shared and pipelined through the computational workflow described above, resulting in the identification of 7668 (peptide-level FDR 1%; average cFDR 0.5%) or 11,275 (peptide-level FDR 5%; average cFDR 2.5%) distinct HLA class I peptides distributed across eleven different HLA class I alleles (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B and Figure 2—source data 3).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: A total of 15,875 peptides (∼79%) were identified from a large collection of 20,176 synthetic HLA class II peptides.
source: To properly assess the efficiency of generating HLA peptide assay libraries from synthetic peptides, a large collection of 20,176 synthetic HLA class II peptides was analyzed by DDA using different mass spectrometers and fragmentation methods (Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—source data 2). Our results show that a total of 15,875 peptides (∼79%) were identified (Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: The pilot libraries contain a total of 223,735 transitions for 26,857 unique peptides.
source: All identified peptides were used to build the HLA allele-specific peptide assay libraries ('Materials and methods'). To date, the pilot libraries contain a total of 223,735 transitions for 26,857 unique peptides and were stored by class and allele in the SWATHAtlas database (Figure 2—source data 5 and http://www.swathatlas.org).
evidence: Data summary with reference to source data and database

claim: The pilot libraries were stored by class and allele in the SWATHAtlas database.
source: All identified peptides were used to build the HLA allele-specific peptide assay libraries ('Materials and methods'). To date, the pilot libraries contain a total of 223,735 transitions for 26,857 unique peptides and were stored by class and allele in the SWATHAtlas database (Figure 2—source data 5 and http://www.swathatlas.org).
evidence: Description of data storage with reference to source data and database URL

claim: 95% of the annotated class I peptides were predicted to bind their respective HLA molecules with an IC50 ranging from 72 nM (for HLA-A01) to 5682 nM (for HLA-B51) at peptide-level FDR 1%.
source: Our data also show that 95% of the annotated class I peptides in this study were predicted to bind their respective HLA molecules with an IC50 ranging from 72 nM (for HLA-A01) to 5682 nM (for HLA-B51) at peptide-level FDR 1% (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figure

claim: HLA class I alleles are associated with peptide-binding repertoires of different affinity.
source: This result supports a recent study indicating that HLA class I alleles are associated with peptide-binding repertoires of different affinity (Paul et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paul et al., 2013

claim: Four independent laboratories generated their own digital SWATH maps using TripleTOF 5600 MS operated in DIA acquisition mode.
source: To promote the worldwide development of SWATH-based MS platforms towards robust quantitative measurements of HLA peptidomes, we assessed whether the HLA allele-specific assay libraries described above could be used to extract quantitative information from digital SWATH maps acquired by different laboratories. Importantly, four independent laboratories generated their own digital SWATH maps using TripleTOF 5600 MS operated in DIA acquisition mode.
evidence: Description of multi-site experimental design

claim: Precursors in the range of 400–1200 Th were divided into 32 SWATH windows of 25 Da.
source: Precursors in the range of 400–1200 Th were divided into 32 SWATH windows of 25 Da (Gillet et al., 2012).
evidence: Description of SWATH acquisition parameters with citation

claim: At an estimated peptide-level FDR of 1%, a total of 3150 unique HLA class I peptides were identified from the digital SWATH map of JYEBV+ cells.
source: The HLA peptidome of JYEBV+ cells was analyzed using the OpenSWATH (Röst et al., 2014) software tool and a combined assay library containing 22,206 transitions for 1507 HLA-A02 and 2194 HLA-B07 peptides—the two dominant HLA alleles expressed on these cells. At an estimated peptide-level FDR of 1% (m-score < 0.01), a total of 3150 unique HLA class I peptides were identified from the digital SWATH map (Figure 3A,B,C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 7 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: Assays generated from synthetic EBV-related class I peptides enabled the identification of one EBV-derived HLA-A02 peptide.
source: Notably, assays generated from the synthetic EBV-related class I peptides enabled the identification of one EBV-derived HLA-A02 peptide (Figure 3C), thereby demonstrating that building high-quality assay libraries from synthetic class I peptides of pathogen origin could be useful for the identification of non-self HLA-bound peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Data result with reference to figure demonstrating proof of concept

claim: Building high-quality assay libraries from synthetic class I peptides of pathogen origin could be useful for the identification of non-self HLA-bound peptides by SWATH-MS.
source: Notably, assays generated from the synthetic EBV-related class I peptides enabled the identification of one EBV-derived HLA-A02 peptide (Figure 3C), thereby demonstrating that building high-quality assay libraries from synthetic class I peptides of pathogen origin could be useful for the identification of non-self HLA-bound peptides by SWATH-MS.
evidence: Inference from experimental result

claim: ∼81% of HLA class I peptides present in an assay library could be extracted from a quantitative digital SWATH map in a cell type-independent manner at peptide-level FDR 1%.
source: High-throughput targeted analysis from these four additional peptidomic datasets indicated that ∼81% of HLA class I peptides present in an assay library could be extracted from a quantitative digital SWATH map in a cell type-independent manner (peptide-level FDR 1%) (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplements 2–6 and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: Most class I peptide precursors (∼98%) fall within the range of 400–700 Th.
source: We next optimized the SWATH acquisition conditions according to the size distribution of HLA class I peptides. Most class I peptide precursors (∼98%) fall within the range of 400–700 Th and were divided in 30 SWATH windows of 10 Da width each.
evidence: Data observation from experimental analysis

claim: Narrowing the size of the SWATH windows by 2.5-fold resulted in a ∼13% fold-increase in the identification of class I peptides.
source: Using SWATH data generated from JYEBV+ cells, we found that narrowing the size of the windows by 2.5-fold resulted in a ∼13% fold-increase in the identification of class I peptides (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figure

claim: The R2 value for SWATH-MS quantification was 0.979 from two technical replicates.
source: The R2 value for SWATH-MS quantification was 0.979 from two technical replicates (Figure 3D).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figure

claim: The dynamic range of peptides quantified in different cell types using SWATH-MS, based on their signal intensity, was about 3-4 orders of magnitude.
source: In accordance with previous studies, we also observed that the dynamic range of peptides quantified in different cell types using SWATH-MS, based on their signal intensity, was about 3-4 orders of magnitude (Figure 3E) (Hassan et al., 2013; Bassani-Sternberg et al., 2015).
evidence: Data observation with reference to figure and citations

claim: A sample of class I peptides from JYEBV+ cells was analyzed in three datasets in SWATH mode, and 2832 peptides (97%) were found in all the SWATH analyses at 1% peptide-level FDR.
source: For this purpose, we prepared a sample of class I peptides by immunoaffinity purification from JYEBV+ cells and we acquired three datasets in SWATH mode. The datasets were analyzed using OpenSWATH and a combined HLA-A02 and -B07 peptide assay library as described above. At an estimated peptide-level FDR of 1%, a total of 2933 unique HLA class I peptides were identified by SWATH-MS and 2832 peptides (97%) were found in all the SWATH analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: Three additional datasets were acquired in DDA mode from the same sample of class I peptides, and 1261 peptides (40%) were found in all the DDA analyses at 1% peptide-level FDR.
source: We then conducted a comparative analysis by acquiring three additional datasets in DDA mode from the same sample of class I peptides using the same chromatographic conditions. In total, 3153 HLA-A and -B peptides were identified at 1% peptide-level FDR and 1261 peptides (40%) were found in all the DDA analyses (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Data analysis result with reference to figures

claim: The SWATH method clearly outperformed the DDA approach for the reproducible identification of JYEBV+ HLA class I peptides across several technical replicates.
source: Thus, the SWATH method clearly outperformed the DDA approach for the reproducible identification of JYEBV+ HLA class I peptides across several technical replicates.
evidence: Inference from comparative data analysis

claim: SWATH-MS has the capability of detecting large numbers of HLA peptides across multiple injections at a high degree of reproducibility.
source: Overall, our results indicate that SWATH-MS has the capability of detecting large numbers of HLA peptides across multiple injections at a high degree of reproducibility.
